title: Semantic chunking
summary: Embed the sentences, compare neighbours and start a new chunk where similarity drops. Boundaries follow topic shifts instead of length, at the price of an extra embedding pass and less stable chunks.
useIf: Long text shifts topic without headings, you can afford an ingest-time embedding pass and you have measured a gain over a simple splitter.
avoidIf: The corpus is huge, changes often or already has structure. Studies have not found consistent gains for the cost.

explain.md: **Semantic chunking** looks for topic changes instead of counting tokens. The splitter breaks the text into sentences, embeds each one (often with a small window of neighbours), and measures the similarity between neighbouring positions. Where similarity falls below a threshold, or a chosen percentile of the drops, a boundary is placed. A maximum size still applies, or one long topic becomes one giant chunk.

explain.title: Semantic breakpoints
explain.alt: Sentences are embedded, similarity between neighbours is computed, boundaries are placed at low similarity points, and a size cap is applied before the final chunks are embedded.
explain.src:
flowchart LR
  A["Split into sentences"] --> B["Embed each sentence"]
  B --> C["Similarity of neighbours"]
  C --> D["Break where it drops"]
  D --> E["Apply min and max size"]
  E --> F["Embed final chunks"]

explain.md: The cost is concrete. Every sentence is embedded once to find boundaries, then each final chunk is embedded again for the index, so embedding tokens roughly double compared with a fixed splitter. Boundaries also depend on the neighbours: edit one paragraph and the breakpoints around it can move, which changes chunk ids and forces more re-embedding.

The evidence is cautious. A 2024 study compared semantic and fixed-size chunking on document retrieval, evidence retrieval and answer generation and found the extra compute was not justified by consistent gains [[tr27]]. That does not mean it never helps: text with sharp topic shifts and no headings, such as transcripts or long essays, is the plausible win. The Architecture Center lists semantic chunking as a custom approach [[tr9]], and the AI Search Content Understanding skill added semantic chunking as an opt-in preview in `2026-05-01-preview` (checked 2026-10-13) [[tr5]].

whereToUse: Transcripts, interviews and long essays with topic shifts but no headings
A small, high-value corpus where ingest cost is minor and retrieval quality is measurable
Experiments against a recursive baseline on your own labelled questions
Preparing text for a later proposition or contextual step on a few critical documents

use: Topic shifts are sharp and frequent
You have a labelled set to prove a gain
avoid: Corpora of millions of documents with frequent edits
Documents that already have usable headings
Teams that cannot measure retrieval quality
flips: A measured gain over recursive splitting appears on your questions: adopt it for that source only
Edits are frequent: choose structure-aware or recursive splitting for stable chunk ids
Cost becomes the limit: lower the sentence window or sample documents

pitfalls.symptom: Chunk counts explode and results get worse
pitfalls.cause: The similarity threshold is too strict, so almost every sentence becomes a boundary
pitfalls.fix: Use a percentile of the drops instead of a fixed value, add a minimum size and inspect a sample by eye

pitfalls.symptom: A single chunk is thousands of tokens
pitfalls.cause: A long, uniform topic never triggered a breakpoint and no maximum size applied
pitfalls.fix: Always apply a maximum size and fall back to recursive splitting inside it

pitfalls.symptom: Re-ingesting an edited document changes many chunk ids
pitfalls.cause: Boundaries depend on neighbouring sentences, so a small edit moves them
pitfalls.fix: Hash chunk text for identity, re-embed only changed chunks, or use structure-based boundaries for volatile sources

scenarios.title: Interview transcripts with topic jumps
scenarios.situation: A research team indexes 20,000 interview transcripts. Speakers jump between topics without any headings. Questions ask what a speaker said about one topic.
unknowns: What does a typical topic span look like?
scenarios.question: How do you chunk?

options.name: Semantic chunking with min and max size, compared against a recursive baseline on the labelled set
options.why: This is the case semantic splitting targets, and the comparison proves the gain before you commit.
options.tradeoff: An extra embedding pass and tuning of threshold and window.

options.name: Recursive splitting only
options.why: Cheap, stable and often close in quality.

options.name: Proposition chunking for every transcript
options.why: An LLM pass over all text for a problem that boundary placement addresses more cheaply.
options.tradeoff: Right for fact-dense reference text with entity-centred questions.

flips.then: Keep recursive splitting and save the cost.
Prefer boundaries that stay stable, or re-embed changed chunks by hash.

scenarios.takeaway: Try semantic splitting where topic shifts are the problem, and prove it first.

scenarios.title: Large, volatile documentation set
scenarios.situation: A documentation platform holds millions of pages with headings. Pages change daily and the vector store is billed per embedding call.
unknowns: What share of pages changes each day?
scenarios.question: What do you pick?

options.name: Structure-aware splitting with a size cap and chunk-hash change detection
options.why: Section boundaries are stable under edits, so only changed chunks are re-embedded.

options.name: Recursive splitting at about 512 tokens
options.tradeoff: Ignores heading meaning and may move boundaries after edits.

options.name: Semantic splitting on every page
options.why: Doubles embedding tokens and makes boundaries unstable under daily edits.
options.tradeoff: Reasonable on a small slice of unstructured pages after a measured win.

flips.if: A subset of pages has no headings and long mixed topics
flips.then: Apply semantic splitting to that subset only.
The stability argument weakens, so retest the options.

scenarios.takeaway: Stable boundaries and low ingest cost beat clever boundaries at scale.

quiz.q: A 50 million token corpus is semantic-chunked. Every sentence is embedded once to find boundaries, then every final chunk is embedded once for the index (no overlap). About how many million tokens are embedded in total?
quiz.hint: Two passes over the same text.
quiz.explain: The boundary pass embeds all 50 million tokens as sentences and the indexing pass embeds the same 50 million as chunks, so about 100 million. A fixed splitter needs only the second pass.

quiz.q: After semantic chunking one chunk is 6,000 tokens long. What is the most likely cause?
options: No breakpoint fired and no maximum size was applied
quiz.explain: A strict threshold produces many small chunks, not one large one. A long uniform topic with no breakpoint and no maximum size gives a giant chunk. Multilingual models and overlap do not cause it.

quiz.q: What did the 2024 comparison of semantic and fixed-size chunking conclude?
options: Fixed-size chunking fails on all tasks
The extra compute was not justified by consistent gains
quiz.explain: The study found gains were not consistent enough to justify the cost. It did not find that semantic chunking always wins, that fixed size fails, or that semantic chunking is cheaper.
